thread.title: There have been a couple of developments which merit coverag

author: Paulo Santos
title: There have been a couple of developments which merit coverag
text:
There have been a couple of developments which merit coverage when it comes to Apple’s ( AAPL ) smartphone CPU advantage.
The Apple CPU advantage consists of an extreme advantage in single-threaded performance, which then translates into a better user experience in many real-world tasks like opening a Webpage, getting better responsiveness from the interface or a smoother experience. It also translates into better power efficiency.
The Apple CPU advantage came into existence with the Apple A6 SoC (system on chip), which was the first CPU using Apple-designed computing cores instead of licensed ARM designs. This SoC was used in the iPhone 5 and 5C. From thereon, Apple expanded its advantage in the following years leading up to the iPhone 8 / X. In the last three years, Apple’s advantage even grew, as Qualcomm ( QCOM ):
First blundered with the Snapdragon 810, leading to an overheating design. And then extended the Android CPU lag by adopting slightly modified standard ARM designs (A73 cores) for the Snapdragon 835. I covered this development in my article titled “ Samsung And Qualcomm Lag: Game Apple .” Apple’s advantage turned so big that during the recent Apple throttling scandal a fully throttled iPhone 7 was still nearly as fast as a Snapdragon 835-based Android phone. Moreover, as I said, Apple’s advantage grew with the iPhone 8.
As a side note here, I consider Apple’s throttling scandal mostly over, as Apple reduced the price to replace a battery to $29 (“near free” when it comes to Apple, so very close to the ideal solution which would be “free”). Apple also loosened the battery replacement criteria, so now any iPhone 6, 6 Plus, 6s, 6s Plus, SE or 7 will be eligible for the $29 battery replacement if the phone is being throttled.
The First Development – Qualcomm Still Lagging Anyway, when it comes to Apple’s CPU advantage we have the first meaningful development: Qualcomm is again basing its Snapdragon 845 on a standard ARM design (with slight modification).
This time, the computing cores will be based on ARM’s A75 design. As a result of this, Qualcomm is promising a 25% boost in performance, and ARM is promising a similar 22% boost in single threaded performance. This development basically ensures Qualcomm will not be making significant headway in catching Apple .
Moreover, since Qualcomm is used by nearly the entire Android world to power higher-end smartphones, this also means Android phones won’t be closing the performance gap to the iPhone. This is so because a 20%-25% performance improvement is something that’s also quite likely from Apple, thus at the very least keeping its advantage intact.
The Second Development – Maybe Samsung Will Leapfrog As always, Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) also will be launching an Exynos SoC for its smartphones. Typically, this Samsung SoC keeps things balanced with the latest Snapdragon version. This is usual - with the Samsung S6 having been an exception because of the Snapdragon 810 blunder - because Samsung sells its flagship in versions powered both by its own Exynos SoC and Snapdragon SoCs, depending on market.
This is where the second major development comes. Samsung has taken the route of developing its own custom cores for the performance cores, like Apple. Qualcomm used to do as much as well, but recently turned to just tracking the latest ARM designs with small optimizations. This is Samsung’s third iteration at the practice. And here’s what Samsung is touting (red emphasis is mine):

A two-fold increase in single-core performance ! Not a 20%-25% increase, but a full doubling from the prior generation (Exynos 8895) used in the Samsung S8 on select markets. If this translates into Geekbench scores, then this will put the Exynos 9810 at ~3,900 points. This still lags the iPhone 8 a bit ( 4,216 ) but it’s already pretty close. Also, the Samsung S9 will supposedly be launched somewhat earlier than usual, coming out in February.
There are many potential implications here:
There a real risk that Samsung will do away with using Qualcomm SoCs again , like it did with the Samsung S6. If not this year, then next, if Qualcomm doesn’t catch up quickly. It’s important to keep in mind that the Snapdragon 835 already is somewhat slower than the previous Exynos 8895. The Exynos posts single-threaded scores ~9% higher. So the new Snapdragon will be improving less from a lower base. If Samsung delivers on its promises, the Exynos 9810 will be around 75% faster than the Snapdragon 845 in single-threaded tasks (though things will be a lot closer in multi-threaded tasks since the ARM A75 promises 34% better Geekbench performance, arguably multi-threaded, and this is close to the Exynos promised 40% improvement). Samsung will build a tangible advantage over the entire Android world . No one else will have the Exynos 9810 or anything closely similar, so basically Samsung will be in an unique competitive position when it comes to hardware. Indeed, Samsung will be more like Apple than ever before, due to this positioning. In terms of what it can deliver Samsung will come much closer to Apple . For some time (and ignoring the throttling scandal) the performance difference between an iPhone and any Android has been real. If Samsung delivers on its promises with the Exynos 9810, this performance differential is nearly all wiped out now. Google’s Pixel line is put in a bad place . Google theoretically has “pure Android” and timely updates as advantages. However, if Samsung delivers with the Exynos 9810, Google will now also have a tangible performance disadvantage . Also, when it comes to Android the update situation is rather overemphasized . A device running Android usually has access to the latest developments in functionality and core apps through app updates, and doesn’t require an OS update nearly as much as an iOS device. Arguably, core apps are updated much, much more often on Android than on iOS. Indeed, the update situation can even be unfavorable to iOS. Take Pokémon Go. You can run it literally on any Android since it supports any version from 4.4 on up. When it comes to iOS, though, the coming February 2 8 update will restrict it only to devices running iOS 11 or higher. Now, iOS 11.x+ is presently on 72.8% of iOS devices, whereas Android 4.4+ is on 93.5% of Android devices. This is thus an example of a popular app actually seeing better support on Android than iOS. This happens often, due to the different nature of updates on each platform. Anyway, and excusing myself for the off-topic, the only solution Google has to counteract this Samsung development is to again reinforce its efforts to also develop its own custom CPU cores . Conclusion Putting it all together, the main conclusions are:
Qualcomm will make sure that the mainstream Android world will lag Apple’s iPhone in terms of performance for one more year . This is so because Qualcomm once again has adopted a slightly modified ARM reference design for its CPU cores. This is somewhat positive for Apple, negative for Qualcomm. SoC designs from Huawei will be very close in performance to Qualcomm’s. Mediatek will be competitive on the segment below the higher end. This is negative for Qualcomm.
